1: [On the Creation 145-146 — The image of God]

Moses says that man was made after the image of God, and after His likeness — not, indeed, that the Creator has a human form, but that the human mind bears His impress. For the mind is the divinest thing in us, and the closest of all things to the Uncreated.

Now Eden is the wisdom of God, a garden filled with plants, in which every tree is a holy word, a thought imperishable and full of blessedness. And the river that flows out of Eden is the stream of wisdom, parted into four branches — prudence, temperance, courage, and justice.
[On the Cherubim 29 — The voice that is silence]

God speaks not as man speaks, with voice and sound, but by pure thought, which the soul hears without ears. The word of God is swifter than all motion; it divides all things, and nothing can escape its reaching.
2: [The Special Laws IV 12 — Every man a neighbour]

Do not despise any man because he is poor or without honour, for we are all formed of the same elements and return to the same dust. If you see a stranger in affliction, remember that you too were a stranger; this memory is the mother of compassion.
[On the Virtues 38 — The stranger at the gate]

Moses commands that the stranger be received as a native-born, and loved as oneself; for the soul of the stranger is delicate and easily broken, and God Himself is called the protector of strangers, of orphans, and of widows.
[Who Is the Heir 60 — The mind's pilgrimage]

The mind is never still. It goes out from the house of the senses to seek what is real, and returns weary, having found shadows. Blessed is the mind that learns at last to sit down, and to be taught from within.
3: The shepherd of the sheep and the steerer of the ship take thought for what is theirs; much more does the Governor of all things watch over His creation. Providence does not sleep, nor does it overlook the smallest sparrow that falls.
[On the Contemplative Life 24 — The feast of the soul]
They gather, these lovers of wisdom, not for feasting nor for strong drink, but to hear the expounding of holy things, and each brings what light he has, and all are made brighter by the sharing.

Abraham sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and saw three men standing before him. He ran to meet them and bowed to the earth. Learn from this, says Philo, that the table set for a stranger may be set for God, and the host who stoops to serve is himself lifted up.
